output:
A Financial Times piece on the proposed Nuclear Energy (Financing) (NE(F)) Bill caught my attention because it would bring the Regulated Asset Base (RAB) model into nuclear power-station financing. That framework is intended to support Sizewell C, the first nuclear plant built in Britain since 1995. Nuclear developments are capital-intensive and often take decades before they become profitable; Sizewell C alone is expected to involve construction costs exceeding £10 billion. Under RAB, investor risk is reduced by levying a charge on consumer energy bills to help fund the build, which should encourage private capital into nuclear projects.

This matters for Ashurst. The firm’s projects practice is heavily oriented towards clean energy, so RAB would give Ashurst and its clients a further financing route for prospective nuclear work. Ashurst already has relevant experience: it acted on the Thames Tideway Tunnel, which used the same funding approach. The Bill may also draw new entrants into the market, expanding energy-sector instructions.

More broadly, the NE(F) Bill sits within a surge of energy investment. The energy crisis has intensified Britain’s drive to net zero by 2050. Keir Starmer has said that, in office, Labour would create Great British Energy as a publicly owned green provider and commit £8 billion to energy projects—another potential source of major advisory work for Ashurst. Yet the sector remains highly policy-sensitive, so the firm will need to stay flexible as the landscape shifts.
